Keep an eye on: Pseudoephedrine is a stimulant, so you might feel jittery, have a faster heart rate, or have trouble sleeping if you take it late in the day. / It's kept behind the pharmacy counter because of federal limits on buying pseudoephedrine. / Not a good fit if you have high blood pressure, heart disease or glaucoma. The decongestant is what causes the trouble there.
Where you can get it: Behind the counter in the US. You need ID to buy it.
Study: Comparison of cetirizine-pseudoephedrine and placebo in patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis and concomitant mild-to-moderate asthma: randomized, double-blind study

What it is for: Extended-release tablet with an expectorant and a cough suppressant for chesty coughs that bring up mucus.
Keep an eye on: The evidence that guaifenesin thins mucus is mixed. Some studies show it helps and others don't. / Dextromethorphan does quiet coughs in adults, but only a little. It won't shut a cough off. / High-dose DXM is a well-known recreational drug. Taking this with other cough and cold products can lead to an accidental overdose. / The extended-release layers only work if you swallow it whole. Crushed or chewed, both drugs get released all at once.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Over-the-counter (OTC) medications for acute cough in children and adults in community settings
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Cold and flu tablet with an antihistamine and a pain reliever, and no decongestant.
Keep an eye on: HBP stands for high blood pressure. It leaves out pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine, which can raise blood pressure. / Chlorpheniramine is an older antihistamine. It makes you measurably drowsy and impairs driving even at the label dose. / Since there's no decongestant, it won't do much for a stuffy nose. / The main overdose risk is taking it with other cold or pain medicines that also have acetaminophen.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Repeated-dose effects of mequitazine, cetirizine and dexchlorpheniramine on driving and psychomotor performance

Generic: Vitamin C 1000mg + Zinc, Selenium, Echinacea, Vitamins A & E
What it is for: Fizzy vitamin C and herbal mix marketed to support your immune system against colds.
Keep an eye on: In 2008 the company paid $23.3 million to settle false advertising lawsuits over its cold-prevention claims, plus a separate FTC fine. / Pooled trial data shows regular vitamin C barely lowers how often most people catch colds. / The echinacea, selenium and other added ingredients don't change that much. / Because it's effervescent, each dose has a fair amount of sodium, which matters if you're watching your salt.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC in the US as a supplement, so the FDA doesn't regulate it as a drug.
Study: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Fast-dissolving zinc tablets you take when symptoms start, to make a cold shorter.
Keep an eye on: These are the oral RapidMelts. They're a different product from the nasal gel and swabs Zicam pulled in 2009 after reports of people permanently losing their sense of smell. / Cochrane's 2024 review found zinc might cut about a day off a cold, but the evidence is low-certainty. / In these trials, bad taste and nausea came up more often with zinc than with placebo. / You have to start within a day of your first symptoms. Taking it later does much less.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US. The separate nasal Zicam products were pulled in 2009.
Study: Zinc for prevention and treatment of the common cold
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Pink lotion that cools and dries itchy rashes, bug bites and minor skin irritation.
Keep an eye on: The pink color comes from ferric oxide and doesn't do anything medically. / There isn't much trial evidence that it relieves itching. People mostly use it because dermatologists have recommended it for about a hundred years. / Versions with added diphenhydramine can cause a dangerous overdose in small children. Plain calamine doesn't have that risk. / Shake it well first. It settles fast, and if you don't shake it you're mostly putting on water.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US, sold generically under lots of names.
Study: Electrometric assessment of the effect of a zinc oxide paste in diaper dermatitis

What it is for: Protects minor cuts, scrapes and burns from infection. It's marketed to people who react to the neomycin in triple antibiotic ointment.
Keep an eye on: It leaves out neomycin, but bacitracin is also one of the top causes of allergic reactions to antibiotic ointments. If it itches under the bandage, the ointment might be why. / It covers fewer kinds of bacteria than the triple antibiotic version, so it isn't automatically the better choice. / There's very little evidence that any antibiotic ointment prevents infection better than plain petroleum jelly.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Topical antibiotics for preventing surgical site infection in wounds healing by primary intention
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Numbs and calms itching and irritation around the outside of the vagina for short-term relief.
Keep an eye on: Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia in rare cases, but a trial of this exact 20%/3% formula found no measurable change in healthy adult women using it normally for a week. / The FDA says not to treat yourself for more than seven days. If the itching lasts longer, you need a diagnosis. / Resorcinol can make broken or scratched-up skin more irritated, which defeats the purpose.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Potential for an external vaginal antiitch cream containing benzocaine to cause methemoglobinemia in healthy women
Journal: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology

What it is for: Reverses an opioid overdose in minutes. It's the second naloxone nasal spray the FDA approved for OTC sale, after Narcan.
Keep an eye on: It's the same drug as Narcan from a different company, with a lower 3 mg dose per spray. Either one is fine to keep around. / Call 911 no matter what, because naloxone wears off before a lot of opioids do. / If opioids aren't involved it does nothing, so there's no downside to using it if you only suspect an overdose.
Where you can get it: OTC in the US since 2023.
Study: The FDA approves the second OTC naloxone - a step toward opioid crisis mitigation

Generic: Vitamin C 1000mg + Zinc + B vitamins + electrolytes
What it is for: Fizzy drink mix with vitamin C, zinc and B vitamins, marketed for immune support.
Keep an eye on: The best trials show regular vitamin C shortens colds by only a few percent, which is a lot less than the packet suggests. / In trials, zinc mostly helped as a lozenge dissolved in your mouth. Nobody has shown that drinking it works the same way. / 1000 mg of vitamin C is half the 2,000 mg daily upper limit for adults. Taking more hasn't been shown to help and can upset your stomach.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US, sold as a supplement instead of a regulated drug.
Study: Zinc for prevention and treatment of the common cold
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: For tension headaches. It adds caffeine to help the acetaminophen work better.
Keep an eye on: Unlike Excedrin Migraine it has no aspirin, so it's easier on your stomach but not as good for migraines. / The caffeine boost shows up in trials, but if you skip a dose you can get a caffeine-withdrawal headache. / Acetaminophen's liver risk still applies, and the 4 g daily limit includes everything else you're taking that has it.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Caffeine as an analgesic adjuvant in tension headache

What it is for: Counter-irritant patch for muscle and joint pain. The menthol feels cool and the salicylate feels warm, which distracts you from the deeper ache.
Keep an eye on: Methyl salicylate is closely related to aspirin. Using several patches at once, or one along with oral NSAIDs, can give you more salicylate than you'd think. / Skin irritation and rashes are the most common complaints, especially if you wear it a long time or put a heating pad over it. / It quiets the pain without healing the injury, so it's easy to keep using a joint that needs rest.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Efficacy and safety profile of a topical methyl salicylate and menthol patch in adult patients with mild to moderate muscle strain: a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, multicenter study

What it is for: Liquid antihistamine sleep aid for occasional trouble sleeping. It's the same sedating ingredient that's in allergy medicine.
Keep an eye on: It's diphenhydramine sold for sleep. The drowsiness that's a side effect with Benadryl is why people buy this one. / Feeling groggy the next day and dry mouth are common, and if you take it every night your body gets used to it faster than you'd expect. / Older adults are more likely to get confused or fall on it. Don't take it with other antihistamines or sedatives.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Diphenhydramine in insomniac family practice patients: a double-blind study

What it is for: Medicated body powder that cools and protects the skin to ease itching and chafing in skin folds.
Keep an eye on: The menthol is the cooling tingle you feel, and it distracts from the itch. The zinc oxide mostly keeps skin dry so it rubs less. / Since it's a loose powder, keep it away from your face and off broken skin. / It only treats symptoms. A rash that lasts more than a couple of weeks needs a diagnosis.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Electrometric assessment of the effect of a zinc oxide paste in diaper dermatitis

What it is for: Pads soaked in witch hazel that soothe itching, burning and irritation from hemorrhoids and around the anus.
Keep an eye on: Witch hazel is an astringent. It calms surface irritation but doesn't shrink the hemorrhoid or fix the pressure causing it. / There isn't much clinical evidence that it works. Most of the support comes from tradition. / Most people tolerate it well, but the tannins can sting on raw or broken skin.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Treatment of Hemorrhoids: Expert Review
Journal: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association

Generic: Dextromethorphan HBr + Chlorpheniramine maleate + Phenylephrine HCl
What it is for: Fizzy cold tablet with a cough suppressant, an antihistamine and a decongestant.
Keep an eye on: The phenylephrine has the same problem as every other oral phenylephrine product. An FDA advisory panel found it doesn't reliably beat placebo at OTC doses. / Chlorpheniramine is an older antihistamine that makes you sleepy, even though this isn't sold as a nighttime product. / The fizzy base adds a lot of sodium, and dextromethorphan interacts badly with MAOIs and some antidepressants.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US.
Study: Meta-analysis of the efficacy of a single dose of phenylephrine 10 mg compared with placebo in adults with acute nasal congestion due to the common cold

What it is for: Fast-dissolving powder with a big dose of aspirin plus caffeine for headaches, muscle pain and minor arthritis pain.
Keep an eye on: Each packet has 845 mg of aspirin, well above the usual adult dose of 325 to 650 mg. The label allows up to 4 packets (almost 3,400 mg) in 24 hours, so it's easy to take too much if you're also using other aspirin or NSAID products. / Like all aspirin, it has a Reye syndrome warning for anyone under 20 recovering from a flu-like illness or chickenpox. Each dose also affects your platelets for about a week, which raises bleeding risk before surgery or dental work. / A 2014 Cochrane review found the 65 mg of caffeine helps aspirin work a little better, but taking it every day can cause caffeine-withdrawal headaches.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as single-dose powder packets in the pain aisle of most US grocery stores, drugstores and convenience stores.
Study: Caffeine as an analgesic adjuvant for acute pain in adults

What it is for: One caplet with a lower dose of ibuprofen plus acetaminophen, so the two work together for stronger relief than either one alone.
Keep an eye on: It's a newer product. It was approved for OTC use in 2020 and only reached shelves around 2022 or 2023, so there's far less real-world history than with plain Advil or Tylenol, which have been around for 40 years. / The label limit for adults is 6 caplets in 24 hours (750 mg ibuprofen and 1,500 mg acetaminophen). That's under each drug's own daily max, but it's easy to go over if you also take a separate Tylenol or Advil. / Meta-analyses show it works better than either drug alone for acute pain, but most of the trials were paid for by drug companies, which the reviews point out themselves.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US in blister packs and bottles. It usually costs more than plain ibuprofen or acetaminophen.
Study: Efficacy and Safety of Ibuprofen Plus Paracetamol in a Fixed-Dose Combination for Acute Postoperative Pain in Adults: Meta-Analysis and a Trial Sequential Analysis

What it is for: Aspirin with a coating that lets it pass through the stomach and dissolve in the intestine. It's meant to cause less stomach irritation than plain aspirin.
Keep an eye on: The coating slows absorption, so it's a bad pick for fast headache relief. You give up speed for something a little easier on the stomach. / A randomized trial found the coating measurably weakens and delays aspirin's effect on platelets compared with plain aspirin, and some people absorb the coated form poorly and unpredictably. / The coating cuts down on direct irritation of the stomach lining, but aspirin's bleeding and ulcer risk stays. That risk comes from blocking COX-1 all over the body, not just where the pill touches.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US as 325 mg coated tablets. People use it for occasional pain, and lower-strength versions are used for daily regimens.
Study: Effect of enteric coating on antiplatelet activity of low-dose aspirin in healthy volunteers

What it is for: A patch that puts a numbing drug right on the skin over a sore muscle or joint. It numbs the nerve endings in that spot instead of treating pain through your whole body.
Keep an eye on: 4% is the strongest you can buy OTC in the US. Prescription patches go up to 5% for nerve pain, so don't expect the same numbing from this one. / A meta-analysis of lidocaine patches for acute pain found a real but small benefit over placebo. It's more of a local numbing aid than a strong painkiller, and it works best along with rest or a pain reliever you swallow. / Not much gets into your blood, but some does. Using more patches than the label says, putting one on broken skin, or using a heating pad over it can push lidocaine in your blood to unsafe levels.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC in US pharmacies and grocery stores as individually wrapped patches. Each one is usually worn for up to 8 hours.
Study: Lidocaine patch for acute pain management: a meta-analysis of prospective controlled trials

What it is for: A counter-irritant cream that makes your skin feel warm to distract from muscle and joint pain. It doesn't treat what's causing the pain.
Keep an eye on: Methyl salicylate gets absorbed through the skin and is chemically close to aspirin. Concentrated wintergreen oil products have killed children who swallowed even small amounts, so keep it far away from kids and pets. / A placebo-controlled trial of a methyl salicylate and menthol product for muscle strain found it beat placebo, but only by a little. A lot of the instant relief people feel is just the sensation on the skin. / It can raise INR noticeably in people on warfarin. The label also warns against using it with heating pads or tight bandages, since both increase absorption and the risk of skin burns.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US as a cream in tubes, along with gel and patch versions.
Study: Efficacy and safety profile of a topical methyl salicylate and menthol patch in adult patients with mild to moderate muscle strain: a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, multicenter study

What it is for: Menthol-scented inhaler that uses propylhexedrine, a synthetic drug related to amphetamine, to shrink swollen blood vessels in your nose and open it up within minutes.
Keep an eye on: Because propylhexedrine is related to amphetamine, people abuse the inhaler by taking out the cotton strip inside and swallowing it or extracting the drug for a stimulant high. The FDA has warned about dangerous heart rhythms, psychosis and hospitalizations from misuse. / Like other nasal decongestants, using it longer than the roughly 3 days on the label can cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa), where your nose gets stuffier once you stop. / There isn't much clinical evidence for it by today's standards. The main objective trial is a small one from 1982, so its reputation comes mostly from decades of use.
Where you can get it: Sold without a prescription in pharmacies, grocery stores and online across the US in the yellow plastic tube. Several other countries restrict or ban it because of abuse.
Study: Nasal decongestant effect of propylhexedrine
Journal: The Annals of otology, rhinology, and laryngology

What it is for: Nasal spray that narrows the swollen blood vessels in your nose. It relieves stuffiness in about 10 minutes and lasts up to 12 hours.
Keep an eye on: The label limits use to 3 days. Past that, rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) is a well-documented risk, even though one small trial found no rebound in healthy volunteers using it 3 times a day for 4 weeks. / It only treats congestion. It does nothing for the cold, allergy or sinus infection behind it, or for a cough or sore throat. / Overuse can turn into a cycle where people spray more and more often just to breathe normally. People call it Sinex addiction, and doctors see this pattern a lot.
Where you can get it: Sold without a prescription at almost every US pharmacy and grocery store in several versions (regular, extra moisturizing, 12-hour). Also OTC in many other countries.
Study: Oxymetazoline nasal spray three times daily for four weeks in normal subjects is not associated with rebound congestion or tachyphylaxis

What it is for: Low-dose steroid nasal spray that calms the inflammation behind allergy symptoms like sneezing, itching, congestion and runny nose. A decongestant only covers those up.
Keep an eye on: It won't give quick relief. The full benefit builds over several days to about 1 to 2 weeks of daily use, so people expecting it to work like Sinex are often disappointed. / In a placebo-controlled trial, about 80% of people on budesonide said their symptoms were mostly or completely controlled, compared with about 23% on placebo. That's a strong result, but it comes from one older study tied to the manufacturer, and nobody has confirmed it in an independent modern meta-analysis. / Nosebleeds, dryness and irritation are common with daily steroid sprays. Aiming it at the septum (the wall in the middle of your nose) can irritate it, which is rare but does happen.
Where you can get it: OTC in the US since 2015 (it used to need a prescription). Sold in pharmacies and online, though the brand name has had shortages on and off.
Study: Budesonide aqueous nasal spray and pressurized metered dose inhaler in the treatment of adult patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis

What it is for: Eye drop that blocks histamine and also calms mast cells, so it stops allergic itching and redness at two points in the reaction.
Keep an eye on: It only treats allergy symptoms. Using it for redness from an infection, an injury or dry eye won't help and can hide a problem that needs different treatment. / In its main placebo-controlled trial, 21% of people on olopatadine 0.2% still had significant itching on high-pollen days, compared with 47% on placebo. It clearly works, but it won't fix everything. / Wait 10 minutes after using it before putting in contacts, since most versions have a preservative that soft lenses can absorb. Mild stinging and dryness are common minor complaints.
Where you can get it: OTC in the US since the FDA switched it from prescription in 2020 (as Pataday Once Daily Relief and Once Daily Relief Extra Strength). Easy to find in pharmacies and online.
Study: Clinical efficacy of olopatadine hydrochloride ophthalmic solution 0.2% compared with placebo in patients with allergic conjunctivitis or rhinoconjunctivitis: a randomized, double-masked environmental study

What it is for: Toothpaste with potassium nitrate, which is meant to calm the nerve inside exposed parts of the tooth so hot, cold and sweet things stop causing sharp pain.
Keep an eye on: A Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials found no strong evidence that potassium nitrate works for sensitive teeth, even though it's the most common desensitizing ingredient sold. / It takes about 2 to 4 weeks of brushing twice a day to fully work, and the sensitivity usually comes back if you stop. / It only manages symptoms. It doesn't fix the cause, like gum recession, worn enamel or a cracked tooth, so pain that sticks around or gets worse needs a dentist.
Where you can get it: Sold without a prescription at basically every US drugstore, grocery store and online store, in dozens of flavors and formulas.
Study: Potassium nitrate toothpaste for dentine hypersensitivity

What it is for: A proton pump inhibitor that shuts down the stomach's acid pumps for up to 24 hours. You take it once a day for frequent heartburn (2 or more days a week), not for a single flare-up.
Keep an eye on: It's slow. It can take 1 to 4 days of daily doses to fully work, so it's the wrong choice for heartburn you have today. An antacid works faster for that. / The OTC label limits it to 14 days at a time, up to 3 times a year. In cohort studies, taking it nonstop for months or years without a doctor involved is linked to slightly higher risks of C. difficile infection, low magnesium and B12, and hip fracture. / Stopping suddenly after weeks of use can cause rebound acid, where heartburn is worse than before you started for a while. That's part of why people end up buying it again and again.
Where you can get it: Sold without a prescription at any US pharmacy or grocery store as 15 mg delayed-release capsules, usually in boxes of 14.
Study: Lansoprazole 15 mg once daily for 14 days is effective for treatment of frequent heartburn: results of 2 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies

What it is for: Once-a-day probiotic capsule with one patented strain of bacteria, marketed to ease the bloating, gas and stomach discomfort of IBS.
Keep an eye on: The benefits depend on the strain and are small. Trials of this strain show measurable but not dramatic drops in IBS symptom scores over several weeks, and the company that makes it paid for much of that research. / The effect stops when you stop. You have to keep taking it, and relief usually fades within days of quitting. / At about $1 a day, it's one of the pricier gut health products on the shelf for how small the benefit is in trials.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC at US pharmacies, grocery stores and online as daily capsules, usually in bottles of 28 or 84.
Study: An 8-Week Course of Bifidobacterium longum 35624 Is Associated with a Reduction in the Symptoms of Irritable Bowel Syndrome

What it is for: Digestive enzyme you take as drops or tablets with the first bite of gassy foods like beans, broccoli and cabbage. It breaks down the complex sugars in them before gut bacteria can turn them into gas.
Keep an eye on: The evidence is small and mixed. The classic crossover trial found it cut how often people passed gas but not the total amount of gas, and later placebo-controlled studies found smaller or inconsistent effects. / It only works on one type of gas-causing carb (galacto-oligosaccharides in beans and cruciferous vegetables). It does nothing for gas from lactose, fiber or sugar alcohols, so it won't help with most other causes of bloating. / You have to take it with the very first bite. Taking it partway through the meal mostly doesn't work, because the enzyme needs to act before gut bacteria reach the sugars.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US as drops or chewable tablets in the digestive aisle of most drugstores and grocery stores.
Study: The effect of oral alpha-galactosidase on intestinal gas production and gas-related symptoms

What it is for: Suppository laxative that draws water into the bowel and lubricates stool. It usually causes a bowel movement within 15 to 30 minutes.
Keep an eye on: It works fast and reliably for occasional constipation, but there isn't much modern trial evidence behind it. Most randomized data comes from premature babies or small specific groups instead of large adult trials. / Rectal burning, cramping or a quick urge to go when you put it in is common and doesn't mean anything's wrong. Some people don't want to use it again after that, though. / Like other rectal laxatives, it isn't for daily long-term use. Relying on it for chronic constipation instead of fixing diet, fluids or the underlying cause can hide a problem that needs a different fix.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC in the US as single-use glycerin suppositories in adult, child and infant strengths.
Study: Efficacy of honey suppositories in treating paediatric functional constipation: a comparative study
Journal: Journal of paediatrics and child health

What it is for: Antifungal that stops fungus from growing, to clear up and prevent athlete's foot, jock itch and ringworm on the skin. It doesn't kill the fungus outright.
Keep an eye on: It only works on skin infections. Tolnaftate doesn't treat nail fungus or scalp ringworm, which both need a prescription pill, and using it there just delays the treatment you need. / Since it stops growth instead of killing the fungus, you usually need to use it twice a day for 2 to 4 full weeks, even after the skin looks clear. Stopping early is a common reason it comes back. / The head-to-head trials against newer antifungals are old and small. Most of the controlled data on tolnaftate is from the 1970s and 80s, though it still works against tinea in practice.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US as a cream, powder, liquid spray and powder spray.
Study: Comparison between undecylenic acid and tolnaftate in the treatment of tinea pedis

What it is for: Antifungal liquid that slows fungal growth, used on tinea infections like nail and toe fungus.
Keep an eye on: Treatments you put on the nail generally have low cure rates for fungus inside the nail itself, because the thick nail is hard for anything to get through. It's weaker than prescription topicals or antifungal pills for nail fungus that's already set in. / It works better on skin fungus like athlete's foot than on nails. Expect weeks to months of daily use before you see a change, and toenails may need to grow out completely (up to a year) before they really look better. / It can cause mild burning, stinging or irritation where you put it on. Don't use it on broken skin, open sores or diabetic foot ulcers, and it won't treat a bacterial infection on top of the fungus.
Where you can get it: Sold without a prescription at US drugstores, big-box stores and online, usually as a brush-on liquid or an ointment.
Study: A new concept in the topical treatment of onychomycosis with cyanoacrylate, undecylenic acid, and hydroquinone

What it is for: Numbing lotion that quiets the nerve endings that send itch signals. It relieves itching without a steroid or the cooling feeling of menthol or camphor.
Keep an eye on: It works well in the short term. A controlled trial of 1% pramoxine cream found itching dropped about 60% within 8 hours, about the same as 1% hydrocortisone. But it only mutes the itch and does nothing for the rash, allergy or infection behind it. / The numbing wears off in a few hours, so you have to reapply it through the day. A small number of people become allergic to pramoxine itself, which can look like the itch getting worse. / Since it has no steroid, it's a reasonable choice for long-term use, large areas or the face, where hydrocortisone isn't a good idea. That also means it won't reduce inflammation or shrink a rash.
Where you can get it: OTC at US pharmacies and online as a lotion. It's different from original Sarna, which uses menthol and camphor.
Study: Anti-Pruritic Efficacy of Itch Relief Lotion and Cream in Patients With Atopic History: Comparison With Hydrocortisone Cream
Journal: Journal of drugs in dermatology: JDD

What it is for: Broad-spectrum antiseptic that releases iodine to kill bacteria, fungi and viruses on minor cuts, scrapes and skin.
Keep an eye on: Using it over and over or on large areas, especially on broken skin or mucous membranes or if you have thyroid disease, can let in enough iodine to throw off thyroid tests and, rarely, affect how your thyroid works. / If you have a true iodine allergy or have reacted to iodine before, avoid it. Skin reactions to povidone-iodine are well documented. / Wound care advice has shifted. Full-strength povidone-iodine damages healthy tissue, so many current guidelines prefer it mostly for prepping skin before procedures and not for cleaning open wounds over and over.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC in the US as a first-aid solution, ointment and swabsticks at pharmacies and online. Clinics also use it to prep skin before procedures.
Study: Effect of povidone-iodine on wound healing: a review
Journal: Journal of vascular nursing: official publication of the Society for Peripheral Vascular Nursing

What it is for: Dilute hydrogen peroxide that releases oxygen when it touches tissue, killing some bacteria on minor cuts and scrapes.
Keep an eye on: Wound care research has turned against using it on open wounds. It damages the cells that heal skin even while it kills bacteria on the surface, and reviews note it can slow healing and make scarring worse compared with saline. / The bubbling people take as a sign it's working is just an enzyme in blood and tissue (catalase) breaking it into water and oxygen. It doesn't tell you whether the wound is infected or clean. / Current advice leans toward plain saline or mild soap and water for cleaning minor wounds. If you use hydrogen peroxide at all, use it once to rinse a visibly dirty wound, not over and over.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC everywhere in the US as a generic 3% solution at pharmacies, grocery stores and dollar stores, usually in a brown bottle.
Study: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2): a review of its use in surgery

What it is for: A patch that releases a steady dose of nicotine through your skin to ease withdrawal and cravings while you quit.
Keep an eye on: The evidence here is strong. A Cochrane review of more than 130 trials found nicotine replacement, including patches, raises your odds of quitting by about 50 to 60% compared with placebo or no NRT. It's one of the better-supported OTC products there is. / Smoking while wearing the patch can cause nicotine overdose symptoms (nausea, a racing heart, dizziness) because you're getting nicotine from both. The label specifically warns against it. / Skin irritation where you put it is common, and the 24-hour patch can cause vivid dreams or bad sleep, which is why some people take it off before bed.
Where you can get it: OTC in the US since 1996 (it used to need a prescription). Sold at pharmacies and online in 7 mg, 14 mg and 21 mg patches.
Study: Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation

What it is for: Aspirin and acetaminophen together to ease body aches, backaches and minor muscle pain.
Keep an eye on: The aspirin raises your bleeding risk, so skip it before surgery or dental work, or if you're on a blood thinner. / It's easy to double up on acetaminophen if you're also taking a cold or flu combo. The liver limit is 4 g a day total, no matter how many bottles it comes from. / Because of Reye syndrome, it's not for kids or teens recovering from a viral illness like flu or chickenpox.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US with no ID or purchase limit.
Study: Non-prescription (OTC) oral analgesics for acute pain - an overview of Cochrane reviews
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Salicylate rub you massage into sore muscles and joints for short-term relief.
Keep an eye on: A well-designed randomized trial found 10% trolamine salicylate cream did no better than a placebo cream for knee arthritis pain. The massage may be doing more of the work. / Try it on a small patch of skin before using it somewhere sensitive. / Using it under a heating pad or wrap increases absorption and skin irritation more than people expect.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC at drugstores and big-box stores with no restrictions.
Study: Trolamine salicylate cream in osteoarthritis of the knee

What it is for: Fast-acting nasal spray that shrinks swollen tissue in your nose so you can breathe through it.
Keep an eye on: After 3 days of use your nose can get hooked on it. Rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) is a common trap with this kind of spray. / It's different from oral phenylephrine pills, which regulators found barely beat placebo. The nasal spray does narrow blood vessels on contact. / It can raise your blood pressure and heart rate a little, so think twice if you have high blood pressure.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US with no ID needed, since it's phenylephrine and not pseudoephedrine.
Study: A randomised controlled trial of nasal decongestant to treat obstructive sleep apnoea in people with cervical spinal cord injury

Generic: Acetaminophen / Dextromethorphan HBr / Guaifenesin / Phenylephrine HCl
What it is for: All-in-one severe cold medicine for fever, cough, congestion and chest mucus in one dose.
Keep an eye on: The phenylephrine in it is the same ingredient an FDA advisory panel found basically useless at normal oral doses, so don't expect much decongestant effect from it. / With four active ingredients in one dose, there are four ways to double up if you also take a separate pain reliever or sleep aid. Watch the acetaminophen especially. / Dextromethorphan gets abused at high doses for its dissociative effects, so keep track of how much you have in the house.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US with no ID needed, since it has phenylephrine and not pseudoephedrine.
Study: Meta-analysis of the efficacy of a single dose of phenylephrine 10 mg compared with placebo in adults with acute nasal congestion due to the common cold

What it is for: Fast nasal spray that opens up a blocked nose when a cold or allergies shut it.
Keep an eye on: It's one of the shorter-acting decongestant sprays. The effect can fade in about 4 hours, which tempts people to use it too much. / Rebound congestion and dependence are the bigger risks over time. / Poison control gets a lot of calls about kids and this spray. A small child who gets into the bottle can become sedated with a dangerously low heart rate and blood pressure.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US with no ID needed, since it's naphazoline and not pseudoephedrine.
Study: Nasal decongestion with imidazoline derivatives: acoustic rhinometry measurements

What it is for: One 24-hour tablet for a stuffy nose plus the sneezing, itching and runny nose of seasonal allergies.
Keep an eye on: Pseudoephedrine raises blood pressure and heart rate, so don't take it if you have high blood pressure or heart disease, or if you take MAOIs. / It can keep you awake or make you jittery if you take it late in the day. / Since pseudoephedrine can be used to make meth, federal law limits how much you can buy each month, even without a prescription.
Where you can get it: Kept behind the pharmacy counter under the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act. You'll need to show photo ID and sign a log, and there's a monthly limit.
Study: Single-dose and steady-state bioequivalence of fexofenadine and pseudoephedrine combination tablets compared with individual formulations in healthy adults

What it is for: Eases heartburn by blocking the histamine signal that tells your stomach to make acid.
Keep an eye on: It's known for drug interactions. Cimetidine slows down the liver enzymes that clear caffeine, warfarin and lots of other drugs, more than newer H2 blockers do. / At the OTC dose it's slower and weaker at lowering stomach acid than OTC famotidine, so it isn't the strongest choice. / High doses over a long time have been linked to breast tissue growth in men (gynecomastia) and other anti-androgen effects, but this is rare at the OTC dose.
Where you can get it: Sold as Tagamet HB and store-brand cimetidine in the antacid aisle, with no ID or purchase limit.
Study: The action of 10 mg famotidine versus 200 mg cimetidine: onset and magnitude of antisecretory action within the first 2 hours after administration

What it is for: Pulls water into the gut and usually causes a full bowel movement within a few hours. It's for when you need constipation relief fast.
Keep an eye on: It's meant for occasional use. Taking it regularly can throw off your electrolytes. / It works fast and thoroughly, so plan on being near a bathroom for several hours after you drink it. / If you have kidney disease, avoid it or only use it with a doctor's supervision, since your kidneys can't clear the extra magnesium.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as a ready-to-drink bottle in the laxative section of any pharmacy or grocery store. Larger amounts of the same thing are used as colonoscopy prep.
Study: Magnesium citrate with a single dose of sodium phosphate for colonoscopy bowel preparation

What it is for: An old-fashioned stimulant laxative. It irritates the lining of the intestines, which causes strong, fairly fast contractions that clear you out.
Keep an eye on: Cramping is common and can be intense. It's one of the harshest laxatives on the shelf and a bad first choice. / It can make the uterus contract, which is why it's a folk remedy for starting labor. Avoid it during pregnancy unless a doctor is supervising. / Almost everyone gets nauseous at a dose that works, and overusing any stimulant laxative can make your bowels depend on it.
Where you can get it: Sold as plain castor oil in the laxative or vitamin aisle of most pharmacies and grocery stores. No prescription needed.
Study: Castor oil, bath and/or enema for cervical priming and induction of labour
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Slows down diarrhea, and the simethicone breaks up gas bubbles to ease the cramping and bloating that often come with it.
Keep an eye on: Don't take more than the label says. Too much loperamide has been linked to serious and sometimes fatal heart rhythm problems. / Skip it if you have a fever or bloody stool. Those point to an infection that slowing your gut down could make worse. / Simethicone is very safe, so the caution here is about the loperamide.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as Imodium Multi-Symptom Relief and store brands in the digestive aisle, with no purchase limits.
Study: Loperamide-simethicone vs loperamide alone, simethicone alone, and placebo in the treatment of acute diarrhea with gas-related abdominal discomfort. A randomized controlled trial

What it is for: Chewable tablets that neutralize stomach acid on contact and calm heartburn, sour stomach and acid indigestion within minutes.
Keep an eye on: Calcium carbonate can cause acid rebound, a short burst of extra acid once it wears off. Taking it all day can slowly make the problem worse. / It counts toward your calcium intake. Taking a lot of doses on top of dairy or calcium supplements for weeks can lead to milk-alkali syndrome (high blood calcium and kidney strain). / The magnesium hydroxide is a mild laxative, so you'll probably notice if you take more than the label says.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC all over the US as chewable tablets in different flavors.
Study: Effects of Aluminum/Magnesium Hydroxide and Calcium Carbonate on Esophageal and Gastric pH in Subjects with Heartburn

What it is for: Tasteless wheat dextrin powder that dissolves completely in food or drinks. It adds soluble fiber to help with constipation.
Keep an eye on: It's a thin fiber that ferments easily. Studies show it doesn't bulk up and soften stool the way thicker fibers like psyllium do, so it's weaker for constipation than you'd guess from where it's shelved. / It's made from wheat starch. Even though it's marketed as gluten-free, people with celiac disease or a wheat allergy shouldn't assume it's safe for them. / Raising the dose too quickly causes gas and bloating, so start low and go up slowly.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as an unflavored powder in stick packs or tubs in the fiber aisle of almost every US pharmacy and grocery store.
StatPearls chapter: The Role of Dietary Fiber in Health Promotion and Disease Prevention: A Practical Guide for Clinicians
Study: Understanding the Physics of Functional Fibers in the Gastrointestinal Tract: An Evidence-Based Approach to Resolving Enduring Misconceptions about Insoluble and Soluble Fiber
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics

What it is for: Antifungal cream that clears athlete's foot, jock itch and ringworm. On the feet it can work in as little as a week.
Keep an eye on: Use it for the full time on the label: one week for athlete's foot between the toes, four weeks for jock itch or ringworm. If you stop when the itching fades, the fungus grows back. / Don't use it in your mouth or eyes or on broken or oozing skin. It can sting on skin that's already irritated. / If it isn't better after 2 to 4 weeks, see a doctor. A lot of itchy rashes that look fungal aren't.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as a 1% cream across the US.
Study: One-week therapy with twice-daily butenafine 1% cream versus vehicle in the treatment of tinea pedis: a multicenter, double-blind trial
Journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology

What it is for: Pads soaked in 2% salicylic acid that wipe away oil and dead skin to keep mild acne under control.
Keep an eye on: It's a mild exfoliant and won't cure acne. A Cochrane review found salicylic acid works about as well as other topical acids, but not clearly better, so it won't handle moderate or severe acne by itself. / Using it along with benzoyl peroxide or retinoids adds irritation without adding benefit. Redness and peeling usually mean you're overdoing it. / It makes your skin more sensitive to the sun, so sunscreen matters more while you use it.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as pads in several strengths at pretty much every US drugstore.
Study: Topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and fruit acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) for acne
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Skin protectant lotion or bath treatment made from finely ground oats. It calms itching, dryness and mild eczema flares.
Keep an eye on: It soothes and moisturizes but doesn't treat the inflammation underneath. Moderate to severe eczema usually still needs a steroid or another prescription. / Oat allergy is uncommon, but it happens. If you get a new rash after starting it, stop using it. / The bath version makes the tub slippery, so be careful getting out.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as lotions, creams and bath treatments under Aveeno and store brands. The FDA regulates it as an OTC skin protectant.
Study: A 1% colloidal oatmeal OTC cream is clinically effective for the management of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in Black or African American children

What it is for: Freezes off common and plantar warts at home. It's the same idea as a doctor's liquid nitrogen treatment, just weaker.
Keep an eye on: The canister only gets to about -60°F, compared with -321°F for a doctor's liquid nitrogen. So it usually takes several rounds over a few weeks instead of one office visit. / Redness, blistering and a ring of dead skin around the wart mean it's working. But if you hold it on too long, you can give the healthy skin around it frostbite. / Don't use it on your face, genitals, moles or skin tags. If you have diabetes or poor circulation, let a doctor do it instead.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC at any US drugstore. The FDA treats it as a medical device.
Study: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen versus topical salicylic acid application for cutaneous warts in primary care: randomized controlled trial
Journal: CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne

What it is for: A few drops after swimming or a shower push leftover water out of your ear canal so it doesn't sit there and turn into an infection.
Keep an eye on: It only dries the ear. If your ear already hurts, drains, or sounds muffled, that's an infection that needs treatment, and this won't fix it. / The alcohol stings on any scrape or irritation in the ear canal. Never use it if you have a hole in your eardrum, ear tubes, or recent ear surgery. / Most of the trial evidence is about treating swimmer's ear after it starts. The case for using this to prevent it is based more on how it should work than on trial results.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC at drugstores across the US, usually near first aid or ear care.
Study: Interventions for acute otitis externa
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Builds your iron back up to treat or prevent iron-deficiency anemia, the most common nutrient deficiency in the world.
Keep an eye on: Stomach problems like nausea, cramping and constipation are normal with iron pills. Trials put the odds of gut side effects at about double placebo. The gluconate form is marketed as gentler than ferrous sulfate, but there's little head-to-head evidence for that. / It turns stool black. That's harmless, but it can hide or be confused with signs of bleeding in the gut, so don't brush off dark stool without thinking about it. / Iron overdose is a serious poisoning risk for kids. The tablets can look like candy to a toddler, and swallowing iron is one of the more dangerous accidental poisonings in children.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US. It's best to get a blood test confirming you're low on iron before you start, instead of guessing.
Study: Ferrous sulfate supplementation causes significant gastrointestinal side-effects in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis

What it is for: Raises your vitamin D levels. Your body normally makes vitamin D from sunlight, and most people who are a little low don't feel any different.
Keep an eye on: If your levels are already normal, the evidence that extra vitamin D prevents heart disease, cancer or fractures is weaker than the marketing says. The biggest trial so far (VITAL, more than 25,000 people) found no significant drop in major heart problems or total cancer. / Where it clearly helps is fixing a real deficiency. Bone health and fracture risk improve in people who are actually low. There's much less reason to take it if you aren't. / It's fat-soluble and builds up in your body, so more isn't better. Taking much higher doses than this for a long time can cause toxicity through high blood calcium. 2000 IU a day is a cautious, low-risk amount.
Where you can get it: Sold everywhere as a supplement. The FDA doesn't check its strength or purity the way it does for drugs.
Study: Principal results of the VITamin D and OmegA-3 TriaL (VITAL) and updated meta-analyses of relevant vitamin D trials
Journal: The Journal of steroid biochemistry and molecular biology

What it is for: A daily dose of the omega-3 fats in fatty fish, sold for heart and brain health.
Keep an eye on: The evidence for heart health is weaker than the supplement aisle suggests. The biggest prevention trial (VITAL, more than 25,000 people) found no significant drop in major heart problems or cancer compared with placebo over more than five years. / Fishy aftertaste and burps are the most common complaint and aren't a sign of a problem. Taking it with food or freezing the capsules helps most people. / At higher doses it can thin your blood a little. Bring it up with a doctor before surgery or if you're already on a blood thinner, though the bleeding risk at normal OTC doses is low.
Where you can get it: Sold everywhere as a supplement. The amount of EPA and DHA varies a lot between brands, since the FDA doesn't check label claims.
Study: Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer
Journal: The New England journal of medicine

What it is for: Makes red, irritated eyes white again fast by narrowing the tiny blood vessels on the surface.
Keep an eye on: Since it works by squeezing blood vessels shut, redness often comes back worse when it wears off. With regular use this turns into a cycle called rebound hyperemia. / If a toddler swallows a few drops, it can slow their heart rate, drop their blood pressure and make them drowsy, because naphazoline affects the whole body the same way it affects the eye. / It's for occasional redness. Don't use it for itching or pain, or for an eye that hasn't gotten better in 72 hours.
Where you can get it: On drugstore shelves everywhere. It's in the same drug family as Visine and Opcon-A.
Study: Over-the-Counter Ocular Decongestants in the United States - Mechanisms of Action and Clinical Utility for Management of Ocular Redness

What it is for: Single-antibiotic ointment for scrapes and minor cuts. It leaves out the neomycin that causes most allergies to triple antibiotic ointment.
Keep an eye on: Neomycin causes most of those allergies, but bacitracin can still cause a skin reaction, and there have been rare cases of anaphylaxis. / A Cochrane review found antibiotic ointments lower infection risk a little in fresh surgical wounds, but for everyday scrapes they're barely better than plain petroleum jelly. / Putting it on wounds that don't need it helps breed resistant bacteria and doesn't do much for you.
Where you can get it: Sold as a single-ingredient ointment, separate from Neosporin's triple antibiotic mix.
Study: Topical antibiotics for preventing surgical site infection in wounds healing by primary intention
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: A B vitamin sold to help hair, skin and nails grow, at doses many times higher than your body needs.
Keep an eye on: A review of the evidence found it clearly helps only people with a diagnosed biotin deficiency or a genetic hair or nail condition. It hasn't been shown to help healthy people get thicker hair. / High-dose biotin can throw off lab tests, especially troponin (the heart attack marker) and thyroid tests. That can make ER results look falsely reassuring or falsely alarming. / Tell any doctor who orders bloodwork that you take it.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC in doses from 1,000 to 10,000 mcg, far more than the roughly 30 mcg adults need each day.
Study: A Review of the Use of Biotin for Hair Loss

What it is for: Daily rinse that coats your teeth in low-dose fluoride to help prevent cavities between dental visits.
Keep an eye on: A Cochrane review of 37 trials found supervised fluoride rinsing cut cavities in permanent teeth by about a quarter. That's a modest but solid effect. / Swallowing it again and again, especially in young kids, can cause dental fluorosis (white spots on teeth that are still forming). It's meant to be swished and spit out, so it's not for kids too young to do that reliably. / It doesn't replace brushing, flossing, or the fluoride that's already in most tap water and toothpaste.
Where you can get it: Sold next to the mouthwash. Pediatric dentists also hand it out a lot.
StatPearls chapter: The Role of Fluoride on Caries Prevention
Study: Fluoride mouthrinses for preventing dental caries in children and adolescents
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Joint supplement that combines two compounds found in cartilage, marketed for knee osteoarthritis pain.
Keep an eye on: The biggest trial ever done on it, funded by the NIH with 1,583 patients, found glucosamine and chondroitin didn't beat placebo overall, whether taken alone or together. Only a subgroup with moderate to severe pain might have benefited from the combination. / Most versions are made from shellfish, which matters if you have a shellfish allergy. / It can raise INR a little in people on warfarin, so mention it to your doctor or pharmacist.
Where you can get it: One of the best-selling joint supplements in the US, sold as tablets, caplets and powders.
Study: Glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and the two in combination for painful knee osteoarthritis
Journal: The New England journal of medicine

What it is for: Lubricant laxative that coats stool so it's easier to pass, usually for occasional constipation.
Keep an eye on: If you take it lying down, or if you have trouble swallowing or a weak cough, droplets can get into your lungs and cause lipoid pneumonia. This has been documented in older and bedridden patients and can be serious. / Long-term use can keep you from absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K. / Not for kids under six, and don't use it for more than a week without talking to a doctor.
Where you can get it: Sold as an oral liquid or an enema. It's one of the older laxatives still on drugstore shelves.
Study: Osmotic and stimulant laxatives for the management of childhood constipation
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Fiber laxative that soaks up water to make stool softer and easier to pass.
Keep an eye on: A controlled trial in kids found it fully cleared up constipation in fewer than half of them. Bulk fiber alone doesn't work for everyone, especially in more severe cases. / Take it with a full glass of water. Without enough fluid it can make a blockage worse. / Gas and bloating are common for the first week or two while your gut adjusts.
Where you can get it: Sold as calcium polycarbophil caplets. It's an option for people who find psyllium (Metamucil) too gritty.
Study: The intestinal ecosystem in chronic functional constipation

What it is for: A well-absorbed form of magnesium marketed for sleep, muscle relaxation and stress.
Keep an eye on: A 2026 systematic review of randomized trials found the evidence that magnesium helps sleep is inconsistent and low-certainty. It isn't supported as a regular insomnia treatment. / High doses cause diarrhea first. That side effect usually shows up long before any toxicity. / If your kidneys don't work well, check with a doctor first, since your kidneys normally get rid of extra magnesium.
Where you can get it: Sold as capsules and powders, and marketed as easier on the stomach than magnesium oxide or citrate.
Study: Magnesium Supplementation for Sleep in Adults: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials

What it is for: Herbal extract used for mild to moderate depression. In the US it's sold without a prescription, but some countries regulate it as a drug.
Keep an eye on: A Cochrane review of 29 trials found it beat placebo and worked about as well as standard antidepressants for major depression, with fewer people quitting because of side effects. That's unusual for an herbal product. / It also speeds up liver enzymes, which can quietly weaken hormonal birth control, blood thinners and a lot of other prescription drugs. This interaction is well documented. / Don't combine it with SSRIs or other serotonergic antidepressants, because of the risk of serotonin syndrome.
Where you can get it: Sold as tablets, capsules and teas. Germany regulates it as a prescription antidepressant, but in the US it's a supplement.
Study: St John's wort for major depression
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: An antioxidant your body makes on its own, sold as a supplement for heart health and for muscle aches from statins.
Keep an eye on: Small trials suggest it can help the heart pump a little better in people with heart failure, but it's an add-on to standard treatment and can't replace it. / Statins lower your natural CoQ10 levels, which is why people take it for statin muscle pain. The trial evidence that it relieves those aches is mixed, though. / It can make warfarin work less well, so tell your doctor if you're on a blood thinner.
Where you can get it: Sold as softgels, usually 100 to 200 mg. It's one of the more expensive supplements per dose.
Study: Coenzyme Q10; an adjunctive therapy for congestive heart failure?

What it is for: Replaces a nutrient your nerves and red blood cells need. It helps most if you're actually low, which is common in vegans, older adults and people on long-term metformin or acid-reducing drugs.
Keep an eye on: A head-to-head trial found high-dose B12 pills worked just as well as monthly shots for fixing a deficiency. People used to assume you needed the shots. / It's water-soluble and basically nontoxic even at high doses, because your body gets rid of the extra in your urine. / If you aren't deficient, taking it doesn't do much.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as tablets, under-the-tongue lozenges and gummies, in doses from 500 to 5,000 mcg.
Study: Effective treatment of cobalamin deficiency with oral cobalamin

What it is for: An antioxidant vitamin that used to be pushed hard for preventing heart disease. It's still sold in doses well above what a normal diet gives you.
Keep an eye on: A meta-analysis of 19 trials with more than 135,000 people found that high-dose vitamin E (400 IU or more a day) was linked to a small but real increase in death from any cause. That's the opposite of what it was sold for. / At high doses it can interfere with vitamin K and raise your bleeding risk, especially if you take blood thinners. / The heart protection it was marketed for in the 1990s didn't hold up in large randomized trials.
Where you can get it: Sold as softgels, usually 180 to 400 IU, and often labeled as natural d-alpha-tocopherol.
Study: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality

What it is for: A B vitamin taken before and early in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects like spina bifida.
Keep an eye on: A landmark randomized trial found folic acid cut repeat neural tube defects by about 72 percent in women who'd had an affected pregnancy before. It's one of the clearest prevention results in nutrition science. / High doses can hide the blood test signs of a B12 deficiency while the nerve damage from that deficiency keeps getting worse without anyone noticing. / The US adds folic acid to enriched flour and cereal to prevent these birth defects, so most people already get some without trying.
Where you can get it: Sold as a 400 to 800 mcg tablet on its own, and it's in almost every prenatal vitamin.
Study: Prevention of neural tube defects: results of the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study

What it is for: A B vitamin sold for nausea, PMS and nerve support, often at doses many times the recommended daily amount.
Keep an eye on: A 2025 expert consensus statement from several medical specialties warns that long-term high-dose use is an under-recognized cause of peripheral neuropathy. That's numbness and tingling that can take months to go away after you stop. / The nerve damage risk shows up with daily doses over time that are well below what some supplements contain, not only with extreme megadoses. / Combined with doxylamine, it has good trial support for nausea in pregnancy. Taken alone at high doses for vague nerve or energy problems, the case is weaker.
Where you can get it: Sold as a tablet on its own from 25 mg up to 100 mg or more, way above the 1.3 to 1.7 mg adults need.
Study: Expert Consensus on Vitamin B6 Therapeutic Use for Patients: Guidance on Safe Dosage, Duration and Clinical Management

What it is for: A supplement made from ginger root that's used to settle nausea, from motion sickness to morning sickness to nausea from chemo.
Keep an eye on: A systematic review of 12 randomized trials in pregnant women found ginger clearly helped with nausea, and lower doses (under 1,500 mg a day) worked best. It didn't do as much for actual vomiting. / It's considered safe in pregnancy at normal doses. The pooled trials didn't find a significant rise in miscarriage risk. / It can thin the blood a little, so bring it up before surgery or if you're on a blood thinner.
Where you can get it: Sold as capsules, chews, teas and candied ginger. You can also just buy ginger in the produce section.
Study: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect and safety of ginger in the treatment of pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting

What it is for: Porous carbon powder sold in capsules for gas, bloating and vague detox claims. It's different from the medical-grade charcoal used for poisonings.
Keep an eye on: A randomized trial of a combination product with charcoal in it did ease chronic indigestion better than placebo, but the evidence for charcoal alone relieving gas is weaker and inconsistent. / It binds to whatever's nearby. If you take it around the same time as a prescription, a birth control pill or another supplement, it can bind that too and weaken the dose. / Charcoal capsules don't detox you. Your liver and kidneys already do that job.
Where you can get it: Sold as capsules, tablets and powders in the supplement aisle. It's not the same product ERs use to treat poisoning.
Study: Efficacy of a simethicone, activated charcoal and magnesium oxide combination (Carbosymag) in functional dyspepsia: results of a general practice-based randomized trial
Journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology

What it is for: Herbal extract a lot of men use for urinary symptoms from an enlarged prostate, instead of prescription BPH drugs.
Keep an eye on: The biggest, best-designed trial so far, a year-long NIH-funded study of 225 men, found it did no better than placebo for symptoms or urine flow, even though it's so popular. / Side effects were mild and rare in that trial, so trying it is low-risk even though the evidence that it helps is thin. / Don't let it put off a proper prostate checkup if you have new or worsening urinary symptoms.
Where you can get it: Sold as softgels and capsules. It's one of the top-selling herbal supplements among men in the US.
Study: Saw palmetto for benign prostatic hyperplasia
Journal: The New England journal of medicine

What it is for: Herbal remedy taken at the first sign of a cold to make it shorter or stop it.
Keep an eye on: A Cochrane review of 24 trials found no product reliably beat placebo for treating a cold you already have. The prevention data hinted at a small benefit, but it wasn't statistically significant. / Products vary a lot in which species, plant parts and extraction methods they use, which is part of why the research is all over the place. / If you have an autoimmune condition or take immunosuppressants, check with a doctor first, since it's marketed as stimulating the immune system.
Where you can get it: Sold as capsules, tinctures and teas. It's one of the most popular cold remedies in the US even though the evidence is thin.
Study: Echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold
Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

What it is for: Liquid antacid with two acid neutralizers and an anti-gas ingredient for fast relief of heartburn, indigestion and bloating.
Keep an eye on: A randomized trial found it relieved heartburn faster than low-dose ranitidine (a median of about 19 minutes versus 70), but the relief doesn't last as long as an acid reducer's. / Magnesium hydroxide can cause diarrhea and aluminum hydroxide tends to cause constipation, which is part of why they're paired. / Be careful with regular use if your kidneys don't work well, since your kidneys normally clear both aluminum and magnesium.
Where you can get it: Sold as a liquid and chewable tablets. It's been a drugstore staple next to Mylanta for a long time.
Study: Onset of action during on-demand treatment with maalox suspension or low-dose ranitidine for heartburn

What it is for: Dark berry extract taken at the first sign of a cold or flu to shorten how long symptoms last.
Keep an eye on: A meta-analysis of randomized trials found elderberry noticeably shortened upper respiratory symptoms. That's one of the better results for a cold remedy, though the trials were small. / Raw, unripe or uncooked elderberries and the leaves have compounds that turn into cyanide and can cause nausea and vomiting. Store-bought syrups and gummies use properly processed berries and don't have that risk. / It's heavily marketed as an immune booster, but there's no good evidence it prevents colds if you aren't already sick.
Where you can get it: Sold as syrup, gummies and lozenges, especially during cold season in the fall and winter.
Study: Black elderberry (Sambucus nigra) supplementation effectively treats upper respiratory symptoms: A meta-analysis of randomized, controlled clinical trials

What it is for: Aspirin with antacids added, marketed as easier on the stomach than plain aspirin.
Keep an eye on: The buffering doesn't protect your stomach as much as the name suggests. One trial found significant stomach damage in about two-thirds of people taking it, compared with about a third on enteric-coated aspirin. / It still blocks platelets permanently, so it has the same bleeding risk as any aspirin. That gets worse with alcohol, other NSAIDs or blood thinners. / Not for children or teenagers with a viral illness. Buffering doesn't remove the Reye syndrome risk.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US as Bufferin. The buffering ingredients (calcium carbonate, magnesium oxide and magnesium carbonate) vary a little by version.
Study: Minimization of gastric damage with enteric-coated aspirin granules compared to buffered aspirin

What it is for: Combines Aleve's long-lasting anti-inflammatory with a stimulant decongestant for sinus pressure and cold aches.
Keep an eye on: Pseudoephedrine reliably raises blood pressure and heart rate. A meta-analysis of 24 trials found it bumps up systolic pressure and pulse even in people whose high blood pressure is under control, and the effect was bigger at higher doses and with immediate-release forms. / Naproxen has the usual NSAID risks, stomach bleeding and kidney strain, and those get worse when a cold leaves you dehydrated. / It's kept behind the pharmacy counter. Federal law logs and caps pseudoephedrine purchases because it can be used to make meth.
Where you can get it: Behind the counter. You need ID, and there's a monthly purchase limit.
Study: Effect of oral pseudoephedrine on blood pressure and heart rate: a meta-analysis

What it is for: Tylenol's pain reliever plus oral phenylephrine for sinus congestion and headache.
Keep an eye on: The decongestant is the weak part. The meta-analysis behind the FDA's later conclusion that oral phenylephrine doesn't beat placebo tested this same dose range and found no real difference in nasal airflow or symptoms. / Acetaminophen still has its usual liver risk, and it's easy to double up without noticing because it's in dozens of other cold and flu combos. / Only about 38% of a phenylephrine pill reaches your bloodstream, which is why this dose does so little. The injected version used for low blood pressure is a completely different situation.
Where you can get it: Sold on the open shelf, unlike pseudoephedrine decongestants, which are kept behind the pharmacy counter.
Study: Efficacy and safety of oral phenylephrine: systematic review and meta-analysis

What it is for: A newer, lower-dose steroid spray than original Flonase. Fluticasone furoate binds its receptor about twice as tightly, so it works at about half the dose in micrograms.
Keep an eye on: The main placebo-controlled trial found clear relief starting around 8 hours and lasting through 24, including for itchy, watery eyes as well as nose symptoms. / It has the same risks as any steroid nasal spray: nosebleeds, nasal irritation, and with long-term high-dose use, some suppression of your body's own cortisol. / It's a different molecule from regular Flonase (fluticasone propionate), so the microgram numbers on the two labels don't mean the same thing.
Where you can get it: OTC across the US since 2018. Look for Sensimist on the label to tell it apart from original Flonase.
Study: Fluticasone furoate nasal spray: a single treatment option for the symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinitis
Journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology

What it is for: The relaunched Zantac, which now uses famotidine after the original ranitidine version was pulled from shelves.
Keep an eye on: It's chemically unrelated to the old ranitidine. The 2020 recall was over a contaminant (NDMA) that could form in ranitidine specifically, and famotidine doesn't have that risk. / In the main multicenter trial, twice-daily dosing clearly beat placebo for symptom relief and for healing erosions in the esophagus, but the trial used higher prescription-strength doses than the OTC label. / You need a lower dose if your kidneys don't work well, and high doses have been linked to confusion, especially in older adults.
Where you can get it: Sold as Zantac 360 across the US. It's the same active ingredient as Pepcid under a different brand and dose.
Study: Famotidine relieves symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease and heals erosions and ulcerations. Results of a multicenter, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging study.

Generic: Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Zinc, Copper, Lutein, Zeaxanthin
What it is for: The exact vitamin and mineral formula tested in the NIH's AREDS2 trial. It's taken daily for intermediate to advanced dry age-related macular degeneration.
Keep an eye on: It's only been shown to help with intermediate or advanced dry AMD. There's no evidence it prevents AMD or helps with early disease or healthy eyes. / The 4,203-person AREDS2 trial found that swapping beta-carotene for lutein and zeaxanthin didn't slow progression to advanced AMD any better than the original formula. The swap was made for safety reasons. / High-dose zinc (25 to 80 mg here) can cause copper deficiency on its own, which is why the formula includes copper.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US as PreserVision. Start it if an eye doctor recommends it. It isn't meant as a general eye vitamin.
Study: Lutein + Zeaxanthin and Omega-3 Fatty Acids for Age-Related Macular Degeneration: The Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2) Randomized Clinical Trial

What it is for: Alcohol-free mouth rinse for dry mouth, with enzymes meant to fill in for the germ-fighting job saliva normally does.
Keep an eye on: It treats the symptom only. Dry mouth usually comes from other medicines (antihistamines, antidepressants, diuretics) or radiation therapy, and the rinse doesn't change any of that. / A trial of this exact enzyme mix found it changed saliva and eased symptoms, but the relief was small and didn't last long, which fits a rinse that soothes instead of cures. / Long-term dry mouth that isn't treated raises your risk of cavities and oral thrush, because saliva normally buffers acid and fights germs.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US as Biotene rinse, gel, spray and toothpaste.
Study: Effects of Oral Hygiene Products Containing Lactoperoxidase, Lysozyme, and Lactoferrin on the Composition of Whole Saliva and on Subjective Oral Symptoms in Patients with Xerostomia

What it is for: Clear, dye-free anti-itch lotion for bug bites, poison ivy and minor skin irritation. It uses pramoxine instead of the pink calamine in the original.
Keep an eye on: Pramoxine is a numbing drug from a different chemical family than lidocaine or benzocaine, so it's a decent option if you react to the -caine drugs. Rare allergic reactions to pramoxine itself have been reported, though. / A randomized trial found a pramoxine lotion beat a matching control lotion for severe itching, but that was in dialysis patients with uremic itch, not bug bites. The direct evidence for everyday use is thinner. / Zinc acetate is a mild astringent for oozing rashes. It doesn't treat poison ivy itself, and a steroid cream is still the first choice for true contact dermatitis.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US. Don't mix it up with original pink Caladryl, which uses calamine instead of pramoxine.
Study: A Pramoxine-Based Anti-Itch Lotion Is More Effective Than a Control Lotion for the Treatment of Uremic Pruritus in Adult Hemodialysis Patients

What it is for: Plain petroleum jelly. It protects skin by sealing in moisture so irritated or healing skin can repair itself underneath.
Keep an eye on: People think of it as inert, but lab studies show it speeds up skin barrier repair and gets the skin to make more of its own antimicrobial peptides. So it does more than just sit there. / It's heavy and seals the skin on purpose, which is why it can clog pores and make acne worse on breakout-prone skin. / It's flammable in large amounts. Keep it away from open flames and supplemental oxygen, which is a serious hazard in homes where someone uses oxygen therapy.
Where you can get it: Sold everywhere, generic and name brand, and it's often the cheapest thing on the shelf.
Study: Petrolatum: Barrier Repair and Antimicrobial Responses Underlying This 'Inert' Moisturizer
Journal: The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology

What it is for: Magnesium sulfate crystals. You can dissolve them in water and drink it as a short-term saline laxative, or dissolve them in a bath to soak.
Keep an eye on: There's a case report of a person who got magnesium toxicity bad enough to need dialysis from drinking Epsom salt. Natural doesn't mean you can take unlimited amounts, especially if your kidneys don't work well. / Don't use it for more than about a week without a doctor's guidance. Your kidneys are how your body gets rid of extra magnesium. / There's much less evidence for the bath soak. There's little proof that meaningful amounts of magnesium get through the skin, so don't rely on it for a magnesium deficiency.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US, usually near the laxatives or in the bath aisle. It's the same product with different marketing.
Study: Epsom Salt Ingestion Leading to Severe Hypermagnesemia Necessitating Dialysis

What it is for: Boric acid capsules inserted into the vagina. They're used off-label to keep recurrent bacterial vaginosis or yeast infections from coming back.
Keep an eye on: It isn't FDA-approved for this. The best study behind it is a small look back at patient charts, not a placebo-controlled trial, so nobody knows how well it really works. / In that same study it worked less well over time. Early on it worked about 90% of the time, but by 36 weeks it had failed in about half. / Never swallow it. Boric acid is toxic when taken by mouth. These are for vaginal use only and shouldn't be used during pregnancy.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC as capsules or suppositories, name brand and generic. Some come with an applicator and some don't.
Study: Boric acid addition to suppressive antimicrobial therapy for recurrent bacterial vaginosis

What it is for: Nicotine replacement in lozenge form. You let it dissolve slowly to dull cravings and withdrawal while you quit smoking.
Keep an eye on: It contains soy, which is easy to miss on a quit-smoking product if you have a soy allergy. / In a large randomized trial, the 4 mg lozenge beat placebo for quit rates by a lot in raw numbers, but the result fell just short of statistical significance. Even well-studied NRT products don't always clear that bar. / It's still nicotine. It can raise your heart rate and blood pressure and has its own risk of dependence, though that's much milder and nowhere near as harmful as smoking.
Where you can get it: Sold OTC across the US. There's no federal age limit, but some states set their own.
Study: A Multicenter, Randomized, Double-blind, Parallel, Placebo-controlled Clinical Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of a Nicotine Mint Lozenge (2 and 4 mg) in Smoking Cessation

What it is for: Concentrated curcumin supplement marketed as a natural anti-inflammatory for joint and muscle discomfort.
Keep an eye on: Most of the strong anti-inflammatory evidence comes from animal studies. The human data is thinner and a lot less consistent than the supplement aisle suggests. / A 2023 meta-analysis of 21 trials found some benefit for joint and muscle symptoms, but the studies used such different doses and formulas that the authors couldn't name one clear dose that works. / Curcumin is poorly absorbed by itself. Products without something to boost absorption (like piperine or a special extract) may deliver much less than the label suggests.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US in many strengths. Check the label for the standardized curcuminoid amount, not just the total turmeric weight.
Study: Safety and Efficacy of Turmeric (Curcuma longa) Extract and Curcumin Supplements in Musculoskeletal Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Journal: Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine

What it is for: Daily calcium and vitamin D3 supplement marketed for bone health, especially for women after menopause.
Keep an eye on: The biggest trial of this exact combination, the Women's Health Initiative with more than 36,000 women, found only a small gain in bone density and no significant drop in hip or total fractures across the whole group. A clearer benefit showed up only in women who kept taking it consistently for years. / That trial also found a small but statistically significant rise in kidney stone risk. / Calcium carbonate blocks absorption of several common medicines, including levothyroxine, some antibiotics, bisphosphonates and iron, so take it a few hours apart from those.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US. Take it with food, since calcium carbonate needs stomach acid to absorb well.
Study: Calcium plus vitamin D supplementation and the risk of fractures
Journal: The New England Journal of Medicine

What it is for: A once-a-day multivitamin and multimineral tablet that people take as general nutritional backup.
Keep an eye on: One of the biggest studies on this, nearly 390,000 adults in three US groups followed for up to 27 years, found daily multivitamins weren't linked to living longer. The adjusted risk of death was slightly higher among people who took them. / It contains preformed vitamin A, and many people in the US already get more vitamin A from supplements than recommended. Too much over a long time can damage the liver and cause birth defects during pregnancy. / It won't treat a diagnosed deficiency or make up for a gap in your diet. It's meant for healthy adults who already eat a fairly varied diet.
Where you can get it: Sold across the US in versions for different ages and sexes.
Study: Multivitamin Use and Mortality Risk in 3 Prospective US Cohorts

What it is for: Trace mineral supplement for antioxidant support. At this strength it's well above the RDA.
Keep an eye on: 200 mcg is more than three times the adult RDA of 55 mcg, but still under the 400 mcg upper limit.
